initial_presentation: A 3-year-old boy, the only child of non-consanguineous parents, exhibited widespread warty eruptions covering the body, including the genital area, but excluding the scalp, face, palms, and soles. The skin changes began at 3 weeks of age, initially appearing symmetrically on the anterior thighs, then spreading to the axillae, and over approximately 6 months, progressed to the current widespread distribution. There was no history of blisters or generalized redness at or after birth. The condition showed improvement during summer and worsened in winter. The child was otherwise in good health with no developmental delays or visual or hearing difficulties. There was no significant family history. Physical examination revealed multiple, bilaterally symmetrical, verrucous plaques following the lines of Blaschko, extensively involving the trunk and extremities. The plaques were oriented transversely on the trunk and longitudinally on the limbs. Hair, nails, and oral cavity appeared normal. Systemic examination showed no abnormalities.

A 25-year-old male of Hispanic and Caucasian descent with no significant past medical history arrived at our emergency department from another facility due to sudden paralysis beginning in both lower limbs. He mentioned having received an intraarticular corticosteroid injection in his right knee less than 24 hours before his symptoms began. He also consumed a high carbohydrate meal within five hours before the onset of symptoms. The weakness in his lower limbs spread to his trunk and both upper limbs.

A female child, aged 1 year and 4 months, was admitted for evaluation of delayed psychomotor development and to undergo surgery for exotropia. She was delivered at full term (40 weeks gestation) via cesarean section following an uneventful pregnancy. She is the first child of healthy, unrelated parents, with no notable family medical history. Upon admission, she exhibited a distinctive high-pitched cry and had a smaller than average head size (microcephaly). Motor function delays were observed, including delayed crawling. She could sit without support but was unable to stand, indicating developmental delays compared to typical milestones for her age. Neurologic examination revealed hypotonia in the left leg, while tendon reflexes and cranial nerve function were normal.

A 14-year-old female presented with a two-month history of itchy skin lesions located on the upper and lower extremities, thighs, and pubic area. Her system review did not reveal any other complaints or associated symptoms. Physical examination showed well-demarcated annular brownish plaques, measuring between 5cm and 7cm. The borders of these plaques were scaly and elevated, with a few pustules observed on the upper and lower extremities, thighs, and pubic area. Some lesions exhibited central clearing. There were no abnormalities noted in the hair, nails, mucosal, or genital areas.

A 13-year-old girl presented with difficulty breathing, subcutaneous nodules, and joint pain over the past three months. The joint pain, which developed gradually, affected her knees, ankles, elbows, wrists, and fingers bilaterally, more on the right side, and worsened over time, impacting her daily activities. The pain was severe at night and early morning, causing her to miss school. Initially, she responded to Ibuprofen, but later it became ineffective. The pain was accompanied by swelling and redness around the joints. Two months after the onset of joint pain, her mother noticed small, round, non-tender, skin-colored subcutaneous nodules on her elbows and arms. Subsequently, the patient began experiencing chest pain and difficulty breathing with exertion, which worsened when lying down. She had a history of an upper respiratory tract infection and high fever (39-40ºC) two weeks before the joint pain, which lasted a week and improved with antipyretics. She visited multiple healthcare facilities before being referred to our hospital. Over the last three months, she experienced joint pain, subcutaneous nodules, and exertional dyspnea.

An 83-year-old Caucasian male, farmer, presented with sudden onset pain and redness in his right eye. He had no history of ocular trauma or previous ocular surgery, and no relevant family history or ophthalmological conditions. He was not on any topical or systemic medication. The patient had been known to the clinic for 3 months with a hypermature cataract in the right eye and a mature cataract in the left eye. He was scheduled for cataract extraction in the left eye first, followed by the right eye.

A two-year-old boy was referred to our department due to a distal diaphyseal fracture of the left femur. He is the first child of non-consanguineous parents. At birth, his weight, length, and occipital-frontal circumference were around the 25th percentile. His mother, a 26-year-old primagravida, had no history of spontaneous abortions, stillbirths, or neonatal mortalities and was married to a 27-year-old unrelated man.
A 10-year-old male patient presented with irregularly positioned front teeth.

A 70-year-old woman visited the outpatient breast clinic due to changes in the skin of her left breast. She observed skin discoloration 6 months prior, which progressively increased, prompting her to seek medical attention. Her medical history includes hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, and osteoporosis, with no previous breast health issues or surgeries. She reported no associated symptoms such as pain, new masses, nipple discharge/retraction, or lymphadenopathy. During the physical examination, her vital signs were within normal limits, and she appeared to be in no distress. The breast examination revealed a single 3 × 3 cm pink, non-tender, raised lesion on the left breast at the 12:00 position. The patient agreed to a treatment procedure and tolerated it well without any complications.

A 41-year-old Japanese woman came to the clinic with a 4-month history of pain in both groins and the right buttock, with the right hip being more painful than the left. She had no history of trauma, alcohol abuse, or steroid use. Her medical history included iron-deficiency anemia diagnosed 2 years prior, for which she had been taking iron supplements. She had no previous fractures, including fragility fractures. Her height was 155 cm, her weight was 42 kg, and her body mass index was 18.7 kg/m2. She could walk for about 10 minutes without assistance, though at a slow pace. Limitations in passive motion of both hip joints were noted: flexion was 100°, internal rotation was 5°, external rotation was 15°, and abduction was 20° on both sides. She could perform a straight-leg raise of the right limb with significant pain. The neurovascular status of both lower extremities was normal. According to the Japanese Orthopaedic Association scoring system for hip-joint function, her right hip scored 46 points and her left hip scored 56 points out of a possible 100 points, with the score comprising 40 points for pain, 20 for range of motion, 20 for the ability to walk, and 20 for activities of daily living.

A 56-year-old Japanese man presented with a 3-month history of asymptomatic brown follicular hyperkeratotic plaque/papules spread across the body, with significant hair loss on the scalp. Some papules exhibited a comedo-like appearance and/or signs of infection. Additionally, there was a slight reduction in pubic and axillary hair growth. The patient had been on dialysis for 3 years due to chronic renal failure. There was no family history of similar conditions, no use of medications related to the symptoms, and no exposure to dioxins.
A 26-year-old female reported experiencing vision loss and metamorphopsia in her left eye over the past five days. Her refractive error was measured at -7.25 D in both eyes.

A 5-month-old girl, born full-term via vaginal delivery, presented with a history of fever followed by seizure and subsequent unilateral body weakness. There was no prior history of seizures, and her motor and language development were appropriate for her age. According to her parents, she was in her usual state of health and behaving normally before developing a fever. A few hours after the onset of fever, she experienced a seizure.

A woman in her early twenties with a lifelong history of alopecia presented with 2–3 months of intermittent, dull, throbbing, and localized tenderness in one of the alopecic patches. The affected area, located on the right parietal-occipital scalp, had been stable in size and appearance since birth. Additionally, three other round patches of alopecia, also present since birth, remained asymptomatic. Clinical examination of the scalp revealed an atrophic white patch of alopecia. Surrounding the lesion, there was ill-defined bogginess extending to the central and posterior occipital scalp.

An 11-year-old male presented to a tertiary care hospital with a history of progressively increasing seizure frequency since infancy. The patient exhibited delayed developmental milestones and right-sided hemiparesis. Seizures were predominantly right-sided, complex partial in nature, and resistant to medical treatment over the past ten years. The child was born at term through a normal vaginal delivery to parents who are not related by blood. There is no family history of neurological conditions.

A 7-year-old boy presented with behavioral issues since infancy. His early developmental history indicated he was the first child, born from an unplanned pregnancy. At 36 weeks of gestation, the mother experienced oligohydramnios, and possible congenital cardiac defects were noted in the fetus. The child was delivered preterm at 36 weeks via emergency cesarean section due to fetal bradycardia. His birth weight was 1.7 kg, he had a delayed cry, and was cyanosed at birth. Cardiac evaluation at birth identified cardiac anomalies including patent ductus arteriosus, ventricular septal defect, tricuspid regurgitation, and a left atrium to right atrium shunt. He was started on digitoxin.

A 32-year-old male reported experiencing chest pain and shortness of breath for the past 2 months. He did not have a cough, expectoration, or hemoptysis, and there was no swelling or lump in any limbs. There was no history of abdominal pain or weight loss, and the patient did not have a history of tobacco smoking or other addictions. On physical examination, his pulse rate was 92 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 20 per minute, blood pressure was 116/78 mmHg, and oxygen saturation was 95%. Chest examination indicated a dull note on percussion and absent breath sounds in the entire right hemithorax, except for the right infraclavicular area where breath sounds were normal.

A 12-year-old female patient was referred to our retina service due to a decrease in visual acuity in her right eye. She had a history of strabismus, hyperopia, and amblyopia in the right eye. Her mother had undergone surgery for skin cancer and maxillary cysts. The patient had multiple odontogenic cysts and scoliosis and had been previously evaluated in Neuropediatrics for macrocephaly. Her intellectual capacity was normal.

A 2-month-old male infant presented with a mass in the right lower limb, noted since birth and progressively enlarging. The mass measured approximately 5 × 5 cm, with a purplish-red discoloration and surrounding tissue swelling. The infant's past medical history, personal history, and immunization status were normal. There were no episodes of cyanosis, convulsions, or bleeding postnatally. Family history was negative for congenital malformations, tumors, or hemorrhagic conditions. On examination, the infant's vital signs were stable, and he was alert. Hemorrhagic spots were noted on the upper hard palate. A 5 × 5 cm mass was present at the right knee joint, which was warm to the touch, of medium consistency, and well-defined. No abnormalities were detected in the central nervous, cardiovascular, or respiratory systems.
A 54-year-old Caucasian male presented with abdominal pain and bloating, for which he had been using nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).

A 59-year-old, right-handed female with 12 years of education presented with a 2-year history of difficulty understanding spoken language. She had a background of well-controlled hypertension for 5 years. The patient reported that spoken conversation sounded like noise or buzzing, especially in crowded areas. She could not understand spoken questions during the interview but could comprehend and respond correctly through lip reading or gestural cues. She struggled to understand television dialogue but could follow foreign movies with Korean subtitles without issue. Environmental noises like doorbells and ringing phones were perceived and responded to appropriately. Her family noted no issues with her ability to express thoughts, recall events, navigate directions, or use public transportation. She managed household tasks, financial matters, and social activities without difficulty. A hearing aid prescribed by an otolaryngology clinic did not improve her comprehension. One year after symptom onset, she began making errors in simple mathematics and her spoken language comprehension declined significantly, though she could still read and write. Her writing style became rough with frequent spelling errors. She occasionally forgot things but it did not impact daily life. She had trouble recalling names of familiar neighbors but recognized them visually. Her demeanor and personal relationships remained unaffected.

A 53-year-old male presented with multiple, dusky reddish nodules on the trunk, persisting for 7 years. These lesions were bilaterally distributed along the lateral sides of the trunk and had shown slight progression. The patient has a medical history of arterial hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. There were no systemic symptoms indicating involvement of other organs. The patient did not report any specific triggers causing induction or exacerbation of symptoms. Stroking the lesions resulted in swelling, itching, and redness of the skin.

A 43-year-old man visited the outpatient endocrine clinic at Tabriz University of Medical Sciences, Tabriz, Iran, accompanied by his sister, for an assessment of skin lesions. The patient exhibited multiple lesions on his shoulders, back, the lateral and medial parts of the dorsal surface of his feet, the medial and lateral malleus of both feet, and the dorsal and palmar surfaces of both hands. His siblings have been monitored in the same clinic for similar skin conditions. These conditions were characterized by palmar, eruptive, tuberous, and trauma site xanthomas, along with elevated levels of both total cholesterol and triglycerides in the plasma. Both parents had normal serum lipid levels. There was no history of coronary artery or other atherosclerotic disorders in the patient or his siblings. The patient reported no other complaints and maintained an active lifestyle as a greengrocer.
A 19-year-old female presented to the emergency room with left-sided chest pain and cough.

A 10-year-old female from a rural area in Kendrapada district, Odisha, presented to the pediatrics outpatient department with intermittent abdominal pain, anal itching, and restlessness at night for the past 2-3 weeks. Physical examination revealed no notable findings.

An 80-year-old woman presented with difficulty in raising her right upper limb, progressive dyskinesia, and gait disorder. She had experienced neck pain for approximately 2 years and numbness in her extremities for about a year, both of which had worsened significantly before her visit. She could walk unassisted for less than 100 meters. Muscle weakness (manual muscle testing [MMT] score: 3) was observed in the entire right upper limb, while strength in the remaining limbs was normal. Hypesthesia was noted throughout the upper and lower limbs. Deep tendon reflexes were increased bilaterally in all limbs, with positive Hoffman’s and Wartenberg’s signs.

On March 7, 2018, a 35-year-old Chinese female presented with a one-year history of persistent erythematous papules and infiltrative plaques on the nose without any obvious triggers. Initially, a hard nodule the size of rice grains appeared on the right alar part of the nose, which was painless and itchy. Over time, the skin lesions gradually increased in size, became thick, and spread across the entire nose. Infiltrating plaques also developed on the upper jaw. Past and family history revealed no similar diseases within the family. Since the onset of the illness, the patient’s urine, stool, and weight remained normal. Skin examination revealed diffuse erythematous papules, infiltrations, and hypertrophic plaques on the entire nose and upper jaw, with a smooth surface.
A 32-year-old woman reported experiencing painless unilateral blurring of vision in her left eye for the past three months.

A 14-year-old male, weighing 45 kg, was transferred to our clinic for further evaluation after being found to have pericardial effusion at a provincial hospital. Initial symptoms included fever and left shoulder pain. Physical examination revealed a reduction in the intensity of cardiac sounds and an elevated heart rate. Notably, the patient did not exhibit arthralgia or abdominal pain at any point during the clinical course.

A 5-day-old male neonate presented with widespread jaundice. He was born at term via vaginal delivery, weighing approximately 2100 g. The mother, with a history of six pregnancies and six live births, was generally healthy except for mild photosensitivity. The neonate had no history of clay-colored stools, fever, or drug administration. On admission, physical examination showed pale conjunctiva, yellowing of the sclera, generalized jaundice, a few red lesions around the eyes, and mild enlargement of the spleen. The pulse was irregular, with a heart rate of about 75 beats per minute.

A one-day-old male infant, born at term with a birth weight of 3.1 kg, presented with no significant prenatal history and an uncomplicated delivery. Since birth, the infant had not passed stool and exhibited increased bilious vomiting and abdominal swelling. The anus was observed to be in a normal position with well-developed gluteal muscles and skin folds. The genital examination showed normally developed male genitalia with no visible signs of a fistula. The urine was clear and free from meconium contamination. A catheter could not be inserted more than half an inch into the anal opening.

A 32-year-old adequately nourished male was admitted with complaints of shortness of breath for 1 month, which had worsened over the past 2 days. He had no other accompanying symptoms. The patient, who worked as a tailor and consumed a mixed diet, was found to be well-built and nourished with a body mass index of 25.3 kg/m2. On examination, he was tachypneic, had tachycardia, and a mild fever. Oral thrush was observed, and scrapings were sent for fungal culture. There were no apparent risk factors for immunosuppressive states.
A 17-year-old female presented with a 7-month history of intermittent swelling in the lower extremities, protein in the urine, and blood in the urine.

A 26-year-old male visited Tianjin Medical University General Hospital due to a painless neck lump, first noticed 6 years ago, which had recently grown rapidly. The patient experienced agitation, irritability, excessive sweating, and discomfort while swallowing.

A 49-year-old male was admitted in July 2010 due to sudden onset of weakness in the proximal muscles of his limbs, affecting both sensory and motor functions. Upon clinical examination, he exhibited muscle weakness in the proximal regions of both upper and lower limbs, accompanied by sensations of tingling and pain. The muscle stretch reflexes in his lower limbs were reduced. There were no signs of upper motor neuron involvement.

An 8-year-old girl from a rural area presented with pain in her left leg and an ulcer on the anterior aspect of her left shin, persisting for 15 days. These symptoms have been recurring over the past 4 years. The ulcer typically healed with antibiotics but reappeared after a few days.

A 72-year-old woman experienced behavioural changes, unsteadiness, and frequent falls over the past year. She had started oral anticoagulant therapy two years earlier due to paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Relatives reported that over the past year, she became more listless and neglected work and domestic activities. She also exhibited hyperreligious behaviour, anxiety, loss of appetite, mild lower limb weakness, and falls. Subsequently, she experienced periods of agitation, confusion, and visual hallucinations, leading to the initiation of antipsychotic medication. Her condition worsened, resulting in the loss of her ability to walk and confinement to a wheelchair.

A 21-month-old male presented to the emergency department with respiratory symptoms. Over the past 10 months, there has been a noted increase in penile size and skin darkening. A sibling passed away 13 years ago with similar symptoms. The patient's weight was 13 kg (Z-score: 1.1, 85.3th percentile), height was 92 cm (Z-score: 2.4, 99.2th percentile), and blood pressure was 139/90 mmHg (Z-score for age-based pediatric blood pressure for systolic/diastolic pressure: 4.3/3.9, 100th percentile. Z-score equal to or greater than 95th percentile indicates hypertension). Physical examination revealed hyperpigmentation of the gums, skin, and scrotum, facial acne, and penile enlargement measuring 8.7 cm (above 90th percentile). Testicular size was prepubertal (less than 2 mL) with no pubic hair.
